overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 15
overview.pill: Using Different Forms for Quadratic Functions
overview.text: In this lesson, students continue to use the quadratic formula strategically (i.e., when other, simpler methods of solution are impossible or too difficult). Students identify the discriminant as b^{2}-4ac and use it to determine the number and nature of the solutions. They understand that the sign of the discriminant can be used to determine the number of real solutions a quadratic equation has, which are defined as follows: a positive discriminant yields two real solutions, a negative discriminant yields no real solutions, and a discriminant equal to zero yields only one real solution. In addition, a discriminant that is a perfect square indicates the solutions are rational; therefore, the quadratic expression is factorable over the integers. Finally, students return to the concept of using the x-intercepts of the graph of a quadratic to write a formula for the corresponding quadratic function which was explored in Lesson 9 of Topic A.
outcomes: Students use the quadratic formula to solve quadratic equations that cannot be easily factored.
Students understand that the discriminant, b^{2}-4ac, can be used to determine whether a quadratic equation has one, two, or no real solutions.
overview.teacherInsight: Emphasize precise mathematical definitions and multiple problem-solving representations. Encourage students to check the reasonableness of their numerical solutions.

exitTicket.title: Lesson 15 Exit Ticket: Using the Quadratic Formula
exitTicket.prompt:
Exit Ticket

Solve the following equation using the quadratic formula: 3x^{2}+6x+8=6.

Is the quadratic formula the most efficient way to solve this equation? Why or why not?

How many zeros does the function f(x)=3x^{2}+6x+2 have? Explain how you know.
exitTicket.solution:
Solve the following equation using the quadratic formula: 3x^{2}+6x+8=6.

3x^{2}+6x+2=0→

x=\frac{-6±\sqrt{6^{2}-4(3)(2)}}{2(3)}x=\frac{-6±\sqrt{36-24}}{6}x=\frac{-6±\sqrt{12}}{6}x=\frac{-6±\sqrt{4(3)}}{6}x=\frac{-6±2\sqrt{3}}{6}x=\frac{-3±\sqrt{3}}{3} or-1±\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}

Is the quadratic formula the most efficient way to solve this equation? Why or why not?

This is a personal preference. Some may consider the quadratic formula to be more efficient, while others may prefer completing the square. After the leading coefficient is factored out, the linear term coefficient is still even, making this a good candidate for completing the square.

How many zeros does the function f(x)=3x^{2}+6x+2 have? Explain how you know.

Since the discriminant of the original equation is positive, 12, and yields two real solutions, the function must have two zeros. OR After solving the equation 3x^{2}+6x+2=0, I found that there were two irrational solutions. This means that the corresponding function has two zeros.
